about: Rules for the Network Scanner Wi-Fi spectrum, Zigbee overlay, channel advice and RF tab. Same {id,text,sources} style as remotes/c4-tips.json, plus 'strength' and optional machine-readable fields. Ids are stable: never renumber, add new ids instead. Research done with web search and direct reading of sources; Apify was asked for but no Apify connector exists in this project.

strength_key.strong: Regulator or manufacturer document, read directly.
strength_key.medium: Credible secondary source, or manufacturer doc with a caveat noted.
strength_key.heuristic: Sonor engineering rule built from the sources and 802.11/802.15.4 basics. Use it, but tune the numbers from real site results.
strength_key.unverified: Could not confirm from a source. Show as a hint only, never as a hard rule.

wifi24.note: Use +-11 MHz (spectral mask skirt) for overlap tests, not +-10.

wifi5_uk.note: Ofcom gives 5730 MHz as the top edge, so ch 144 (5710-5730) fits. Ch 120-128 sit on weather radar (5600-5650); ETSI DFS needs a 10 minute check there, so many APs skip them.
Licence-exempt indoors at 200 mW, DFS removed July 2020. Ch 169/173 are outside 5850 and not allowed. Many APs with a GB country code still hide 149-165 on older firmware.

wifi6_uk.upper_6ghz: 6425-7125 MHz not opened for Wi-Fi in the sources read. Treat as not allowed.

rf_subghz.notes: Somfy quotes up to 65 ft (about 20 m), through walls.
Check the model label. UK RA2/RA3 are not Caseta.

wifi.text: 2.4 GHz: put every AP on 1, 6 or 11 at 20 MHz. Never 40 MHz on 2.4 GHz. Odd channels like 2, 3, 9 overlap two neighbours at once.

UK allows 2.4 GHz channels 12 and 13. Flag any neighbour on 12 or 13: it lands on Zigbee 22-26 and weakens the usual Zigbee 25 choice. Don't use 12/13 for our own APs (some clients won't connect and it breaks the 1/6/11 grid).

Co-channel contention: a BSS on the same channel heard above -82 dBm (20 MHz) makes our AP wait its turn (802.11 preamble detect). Count same-channel BSSs above -82 dBm as contenders; between -82 and -90 dBm count at half weight; ignore below -90 dBm.
sources: 802.11 CCA: -82 dBm preamble detect, -62 dBm energy detect (IEEE 802.11-2020 clause 17.3.10.6)

wifi.text: Adjacent overlap (e.g. a neighbour on 3 next to our 1): the AP can't decode it, so it only defers above about -62 dBm, and below that the neighbour is raw noise. Weight an overlapping, non-identical channel by the share of the 22 MHz that overlaps, and treat anything above -62 dBm as a red flag.

Channel score (lower is better): for each candidate channel, sum over every scanned BSS (excluding our own SSIDs' BSSIDs on that AP) weight(rssi) x overlap(channel, bss span). weight = 10^((rssi+95)/10) clipped so anything under -90 dBm adds 0. Add the measured channel utilisation (if the AP reports it) and a penalty for DFS when the job needs never-interrupted AV. Recommend the lowest score; show the top 3 with reasons.

Our own APs: neighbouring APs never on the same channel; on 5 GHz, two of our APs may share a channel only if each hears the other below -85 dBm. 'Place APs on channels as far apart from each other as possible.'
5 GHz width: 1-2 APs and a quiet band, use 80 MHz; 3+ APs or busy neighbours, use 40 MHz; very busy flats/offices, 20 MHz.

For AV and control (Control4, Sonos, streaming) prefer non-DFS 36-48 and 149-165. DFS channels cost a 60 s silent check at start (10 min on 120-128) and a forced move plus 30 min block if radar is heard.
Use DFS (52-144) to add capacity when there are 3+ APs, but only after the AP's log shows no radar events for a week. Near airports, coasts and weather radar, keep critical SSIDs off DFS.

Before recommending 149-165, check the AP model and firmware supports them with country GB. If not, recommend 36-48 then DFS. UK indoor use of 149-165 is legal (Ofcom, 200 mW, no DFS since July 2020); one OpenWrt thread claims otherwise but cites no Ofcom document.

6 GHz (UK 5925-6425 MHz only): 80 MHz by default (6 clean 80 MHz channels), 160 MHz only with 1-2 APs (3 channels). Use Preferred Scanning Channels (PSC: 5, 21, 37, 53, 69, 85) for 20 MHz primaries so clients find the AP fast.
6 GHz indoor LPI max 250 mW EIRP, so plan 6 GHz cells smaller than 5 GHz; don't expect one 6 GHz AP to cover a house. Upper 6 GHz (6425-7125) is not open to Wi-Fi in the sources read.
Signal grades for the walk test: -30 to -50 excellent, -50 to -67 good, -67 is the minimum for voice/video/AV, -67 to -75 fair, -75 to -80 weak, below -80 bad. SNR at least 25 dB.
Don't trust AP auto-channel on its own: many pick only at boot. Re-run the scanner's recommendation at handover and after neighbours change.
Sonos SonosNet (wired Sonos + others meshed) runs on 2.4 GHz 1, 6 or 11. Set it to a different channel from the nearest AP's 2.4 GHz radio, and keep it clear of the Control4 Zigbee channel.
sources: Sonos support: SonosNet channel settings (not read in this research; widely documented)

wifi.text: Android limits a foreground app to 4 Wi-Fi scans per 2 minutes. For a 'live' meter on the site tablets, turn off Wi-Fi scan throttling in Developer options (Google Workspace can't set it), or the chart updates only every 30 s.

A passive scan gives BSSID, SSID, frequency, RSSI and (Android ScanResult / nmcli / CoreWLAN) channel width and centre frequency. Use centre + width, not primary channel, when testing overlap, or 40/80 MHz neighbours look narrower than they are.

zigbee.text: Control4: pick 15, 20 or 25 deliberately; never leave the default. These sit between Wi-Fi 1, 6 and 11.
Control4's mesh picks the least-used channel once, at mesh creation, and never re-checks. So a scan at handover and on service visits is the only check.

Overlap test: Zigbee centre 2405+5(k-11) MHz; Wi-Fi 20 MHz ch n spans (2407+5n) +-11 MHz. With that: Wi-Fi 1 hits Zigbee 11-14, Wi-Fi 6 hits 16-19, Wi-Fi 11 hits 21-24, Wi-Fi 13 hits 22-26. 15, 20, 25 are clear of 1/6/11; 25 is lost if anyone uses Wi-Fi 12 or 13.

Zigbee pick: score each of 15, 20, 25 (and 11-26 for Thread) as the sum of weight(rssi) for every Wi-Fi BSS whose span covers the channel centre +-1 MHz, plus measured 802.15.4 energy if a probe is present. Prefer 15/20/25 in that score order. Explain the pick in words, e.g. 'Zigbee 20: no Wi-Fi above -85 dBm overlaps it.'
Keep every Wi-Fi AP or router at least 5 m (15 ft) from the Control4 mesh controller. A nearby AP can block Zigbee even on a channel far away (receiver overload).
Never put the mesh controller in a rack; use a secondary controller centrally, or the C4-AK-3M 3 m antenna kit.
Max 70 nodes per Control4 mesh; add mesh controllers beyond that. Plan 5-9 m between Zigbee devices.
Never use Wi-Fi on a Control4 mesh controller; wire it.

Other 802.15.4 networks share these channels: Philips Hue (defaults 11/15/20/25), Thread (Apple, Google, Matter), Lutron Clear Connect Type X, IKEA, Hive. Only a 802.15.4 energy scan sees them; a Wi-Fi scan can't. If the Hue bridge is on the same channel as Control4, move Hue.

Thread uses channels 11-26 like Zigbee. Apple and Google pick the Thread channel themselves; Home Assistant users can set it. Use the same Wi-Fi-clear rule (15/20/25) and keep Thread off the Control4 channel.

Non-Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz sources: Bluetooth (hops all band), microwave ovens (strongest around 2450-2460 MHz, Zigbee 19-21), analogue baby monitors and AV senders, wireless speakers. UK DECT phones are 1880-1900 MHz and don't affect Zigbee (the US 5.8 GHz/DECT 6.0 tip doesn't apply).
Control4 recommends a 24 hour 2.4 GHz spectrum scan (they name MetaGeek Wi-Spy) where interference is suspected.

rf.text: Bond Bridge: mDNS _bond._tcp (TXT carries version). HTTP GET /v2/sys/version needs no token: returns target, fw_ver, fw_date, make, model, uptime_s. Everything else needs the BOND-Token header (from /v2/token within 10 min of a power cycle). Some APs drop the mDNS reply; a power cycle often makes it appear. See disc.bond for DHCP/OUI matching.
Somfy TaHoma / Connexoon: see disc.tahoma (newer, from the Home Assistant manifest). _kizbox._tcp always; the local API on 8443 (_kizboxdev._tcp) appears only after Developer Mode is on.
Somfy myLink (RTS to Wi-Fi): JSON-RPC on TCP 44100 with the system ID set in the myLink app. No reliable mDNS name; identify by OUI/hostname and a TCP 44100 probe.
sources: Integration docs (Home Assistant somfy_mylink) - port not re-read in this research

rf.text: Lutron RA2 Select / RA3 / Caseta processors: mDNS _lutron._tcp; LEAP on TCP 8081 (TLS). RA2 main repeater: Telnet 23. See disc.lutron for TXT keys; pairing is on 8083.
sources: Home Assistant lutron_caseta / lutron integrations (not re-read here)

rf.text: Philips Hue bridge: mDNS _hue._tcp; GET /api/config without a key gives name, bridgeid, swversion (no Zigbee channel without a key).
sources: Philips Hue developer docs (not re-read here)

rf.text: Also look for: Shelly (_shelly._tcp, Gen2+ /rpc/Shelly.GetDeviceInfo), Thread border routers (_meshcop._udp), Matter (_matter._tcp), HomeKit (_hap._tcp), Control4 (SDDP UDP 1902, already in the scanner).

Somfy RTS (433.42 MHz, one-way): Somfy quotes up to 65 ft (about 20 m), omnidirectional, through walls. Treat 20 m with no more than two internal walls as the design limit; metal blinds, foil-backed plasterboard, concrete and steel lintels shorten it a lot.
RTS has no feedback: a missed command looks like a stuck blind. Any blind that fails the probe test needs a bridge/transmitter moved, an extra RTS transmitter, or a wired/io option.

Bond Bridge: place centrally, high, out of racks and metal boxes, with line of sight to as many motors as practical. One Bond covers a typical floor; add a second Bond (Bond Pro or extra bridge) per floor when the probe shows marginal results.

Lutron Clear Connect Type A: every device within 30 ft (9 m) of the hub or a repeater; repeaters within 60 ft (18 m) of each other. Never in a metal enclosure. Grounded metal back boxes, metal plates, ductwork and fridges cause problems.
UK/EU Lutron systems use the 868 MHz band, not 434 MHz (US). A 433 MHz probe will not measure them; read the frequency on the model label.

CC1101 RSSI to dBm: read RSSI register as a byte; if >= 128, dBm = (byte-256)/2 - offset, else dBm = byte/2 - offset. Offset is about 74 dB at 433 MHz (datasheet table). Absolute accuracy is only a few dB; relative readings on the same unit are good.

CC1101 sensitivity: -116 dBm at 0.6 kBaud, 433 MHz. Bands 300-348, 387-464, 779-928 MHz. In homes the real noise floor at 433 MHz with a 100 kHz RX filter is usually -100 to -105 dBm; measure it on each site rather than assume.

433 MHz probe grades (measured RSSI of real RTS/Bond frames at the blind, plus margin over the measured floor): solid = at least -80 dBm and 20 dB over the floor; marginal = -80 to -95 dBm or 10-20 dB margin; fail = below -95 dBm or under 10 dB margin. Grade on the worse of the two. Show the margin, because cheap modules differ in absolute dBm.

At 433 MHz the usual interferers are car key fobs, weather stations, doorbells, alarm sensors and other 433.92 MHz gadgets, plus noise from LED drivers and switch-mode PSUs near motors. Sample the floor for 60 s and flag anything more than 10 dB above the median.

Radio for the portable probe: CC1101 (TI) on an ESP32. Use the E07-M1101D-SMA module (SMA, 433 MHz matched) with a quarter-wave 17 cm whip; ESPSomfy-RTS found cheap blue boards can have under 15 ft range. Not RXB6 (no RSSI output, receive only). SX1278/Ra-02 also gives RSSI in OOK mode (RadioLib) but most ESPSomfy-style RTS code expects CC1101.

Libraries: SmartRC-CC1101-Driver-Lib (used by ESPSomfy-RTS, has getRssi) or RadioLib (CC1101 and SX127x, getRSSI). ESPSomfy-RTS already decodes RTS frames, so the probe can show RSSI per Somfy remote/address, not just raw carrier.
For io-homecontrol, Velux io and UK Lutron (868 MHz) the same CC1101 chip works, but buy the 868 MHz matched module and antenna; one module can't serve both bands well.

hardware.text: ESP32-C6 (about £8-15 dev board): Wi-Fi 6 2.4 GHz + 802.15.4 + BLE. Call esp_ieee802154_energy_detect(duration in 16 us symbols) per channel 11-26; result arrives in esp_ieee802154_energy_detect_done(int8 dBm). The ieee802154_cli example has 'ed -d <symbols>'. Best cheap way to add a real Zigbee/Thread energy bar to the chart. ESP32-H2 does 802.15.4 + BLE only (no Wi-Fi), fine as a USB dongle on the Pi.
Alternative: Sonoff ZBDongle-P/E or similar on the Site Rig Pi; zigpy/ZHA 'energy scan' gives per-channel energy 11-26 without custom firmware.
sources: Home Assistant ZHA docs (not re-read here)

hardware.text: RTL-SDR V3/V4 (about £30-40): good for 433/868 MHz on the Pi (rtl_power waterfall). It can't reach 2.4 GHz (tuner tops out around 1.7-1.8 GHz).

HackRF One (about £300+): 1 MHz-6 GHz, hackrf_sweep outputs CSV rows of dB per bin, fast enough for a live 2.4 and 5 GHz waterfall on a Pi 5. Not calibrated; good for shapes (microwave, video sender), not exact dBm. Misses most of 6 GHz Wi-Fi.
tinySA Ultra (about £120-150): handheld 100 kHz-5.3 GHz analyser with USB serial control; can be scripted from the Pi for 433/868/2.4 GHz. Middle ground between RTL-SDR and HackRF.
Wi-Spy Lucid: $999, 2.2-7.25 GHz, covers 2.4/5/6 GHz, Chanalyzer runs on Windows and macOS only (not Pi or Android). The tool Control4 names. Worth one for the office kit, not for every van.

Recommended stack: (1) Wi-Fi scan from the tablet/laptop for SSIDs and channels (free, now); (2) ESP32-C6 probe for Zigbee/Thread energy (cheap, high value); (3) CC1101 433 MHz probe for RTS/Bond (cheap, high value); (4) RTL-SDR on the Site Rig for sub-GHz waterfall; (5) HackRF or Wi-Spy only for problem sites.

presentation.text: Spectrum chart: one curve per BSS spanning its true width (centre +- width/2), height = RSSI, our SSIDs highlighted, neighbours grey. This is the familiar Wi-Fi Analyzer look engineers expect.
Overlay Zigbee 11-26 as thin 2 MHz bars on the 2.4 GHz axis, the Control4 mesh channel in brand colour, with ESP32-C6 energy (if present) as bar height.
Add a time graph (RSSI per BSS over the last few minutes) and, when a probe/SDR is connected, a waterfall. Waterfalls show non-Wi-Fi sources (microwave, video senders) that a scan can't.
Show advice as plain sentences with a reason and a grade, e.g. 'Move 2.4 GHz to 11: channel 6 has 4 neighbours above -75 dBm.' Never just stars. Show the top 3 options so the engineer can choose.
Colour lines on the chart at -67 dBm (AV minimum) and -82 dBm (contention threshold).

zigbee_meter.text: Probe chip: ESP32-C6 is fine if it sweeps 802.15.4 while its Wi-Fi is idle (connected but not scanning). Espressif rates Wi-Fi scanning alongside Zigbee/Thread scanning as 'supported but unstable', and 802.15.4 receive has the lowest priority on the shared 2.4 GHz radio. For an always-listening node meter, ESP32-H2 (802.15.4 + BLE, no Wi-Fi) or a C6/S3 + H2 pair is cleaner. Rule for the firmware: never run a Wi-Fi scan during a Zigbee sweep or listen window.

Alternatives: nRF52840 dongle (about £10-15, Nordic sniffer + Wireshark extcap, per-packet power in dBm, good for deep capture in the office). Silicon Labs EFR32 dongles (ZBDongle-E): energy scan maxRssiValue in dBm. TI CC2652 (ZBDongle-P) via zigpy: energy scan is a percentage, not dBm, so don't mix it with dBm grades. Keep the ESP32 probe as the site tool; it shares the Remotes/RF probe firmware pattern.

ESP-IDF receive: esp_ieee802154_receive_done(uint8_t *frame, esp_ieee802154_frame_info_t *info). frame[0] is the PSDU length; the FCS bytes are replaced by RSSI and LQI. info has channel, rssi (int8 dBm), lqi, pending, timestamp. You MUST call esp_ieee802154_receive_handle_done(frame) after copying (required since IDF 5.1.3) or the driver runs out of buffers and RX stops. Callbacks run in ISR context: copy into a queue, parse in a task.

Energy detect: esp_ieee802154_energy_detect(duration) takes 16 us symbols (e.g. 500 = 8 ms); the result comes in esp_ieee802154_energy_detect_done(int8_t dBm). Set the channel with esp_ieee802154_set_channel(11-26) before each call. Take several samples per channel and report max and median; a single 8 ms window misses bursty Wi-Fi.

Node meter: esp_ieee802154_set_promiscuous(true) + esp_ieee802154_set_rx_when_idle(true) on the mesh channel, then group frames by source address (short + PAN ID; extended address when present) and keep last/avg RSSI and LQI per node.

Beacon request: bytes 03 08 <seq> FF FF FF FF 07 (FC 0x0803 MAC command, dst PAN 0xFFFF, dst addr 0xFFFF, cmd 0x07), sent with esp_ieee802154_transmit(frame, false). Listen about 200-300 ms per channel for beacons (FC low 3 bits = 0). The build's format is correct.

Zigbee beacon payload (protocol ID 0x00): stack profile (2 = Zigbee PRO), protocol version, router capacity, device depth, end-device capacity, 8-byte extended PAN ID, tx offset, nwkUpdateId. Permit-join = bit 15 of the superframe spec (0xCFFF yes, 0x4FFF no). Show 'joining open' as a warning: someone left permit-join on.

Thread: routers do answer a beacon request, but since Thread 1.2.1 the beacon has no payload (no network name, no ext PAN). Classify a beacon with no Zigbee payload as 'Thread / other 802.15.4', keep its 16-bit PAN ID, and name it from the LAN (_meshcop._udp TXT nn = network name, xp = ext PAN ID). Thread is also visible passively from MLE Advertisements (about every 30 s) on its channel.

What an active beacon scan finds: Zigbee coordinators and routers that allow beacons (Control4, Hue, IKEA, Aqara, SmartThings, neo if it is Zigbee) - yes, from routers in earshot. End-devices never answer. Lutron Clear Connect Type X is Thread-based (standard 802.15.4 + 6LoWPAN), so it shows as Thread. Sleepy-only networks or a hub out of range show nothing: say 'not heard here', not 'not present'.

Labelling meshes by ext PAN ID OUI is a hint only: no source confirms Control4 or Hue use the coordinator EUI-64 as the ext PAN ID. Known OUIs: Control4 00:0F:FF, Philips/Signify 00:17:88 (confirmed as MAC OUIs). Also check the beacon's source extended address (if long-addressed) and the router addresses heard in promiscuous mode. Best label = channel match with a hub found on the LAN (zbm.lan.*). Show 'probably Control4' unless two signals agree.

Heatmiser: no Heatmiser IEEE OUI or Zigbee address capture was found. Its docs never say 'Zigbee' (they say 'Mesh'), though the Home Assistant integration exposes a 'ZigBee Channel' and the API has SET_CHANNEL. Don't hard-code a Heatmiser OUI; identify neo meshes by matching the channel read from the neoHub API.

Hue channel with no probe: CLIP v1 GET /api/<appkey>/config -> zigbeechannel (11/15/20/25, 0 = not set); CLIP v2 /clip/v2/resource/zigbee_connectivity -> channel.value 'channel_NN'. Needs an app key (press the bridge button once; store the key in the project's Network Map record so nobody types it again). The keyless /api/config probably doesn't include it. The channel can be changed with PUT config {zigbeechannel:N}.

neoHub channel with no probe: Home Assistant's heatmiserneo integration shows a 'ZigBee Channel' diagnostic read from the hub. Most likely from {"GET_SYSTEM":0} (field not confirmed). Legacy TCP 4242 needs no token (send JSON + NUL byte); WebSocket 4243 needs the API token made in the Heatmiser app (Settings > System > API Access). New firmware turns 4242 off after 48 h idle unless 'Legacy API Enable' is on. SET_CHANNEL exists to move it.

Control4 Zigbee channel: set and shown only in Composer Pro (Zigbee Channel on the mesh controller). No public LAN API, SDDP field or Director endpoint exposes it. So: probe it (beacon scan) or pick it from a dropdown once and save it in the project's Network Map record; then every app reads it from there.

Node RSSI grades: Solid >= -75 dBm, Marginal -75 to -85, Poor below -85. This matches Silicon Labs' example of 20 dB margin over a typical -95 dBm receiver (-75) and 10 dB margin (-85); ZHA calls -60 and above strong and -80 and below at risk. The build's draft numbers are good. Grade on RSSI; ignore LQI as a grade (vendors compute it differently).

Channel energy grades from ED (dBm, max over samples): clear below -85, busy -85 to -70, bad above -70. Use the median for the background and max for bursts. A Zigbee channel whose median is within 10 dB of the mesh's weakest node RSSI is a failing channel.

Heatmiser neo: neoHub Gen3 has two radios, 2.4 GHz (the neoStat mesh) and 868 MHz (neoAir/RF kit). The neoHub mini lists only 868 MHz. Up to 32 devices per hub, about 40 m in open space. Mains-powered neoStats form the mesh; battery neoAir joins but doesn't repeat; neoPlug and Boost repeat both mesh and RF. Advice: at least one mains device or neoPlug per floor, more through thick walls or metal; hub is wired to the router.

No-typing flow: (1) LAN scan finds hubs (Control4 SDDP/SSDP, Hue, neoHub, Dirigera, TaHoma, Bond, Lutron, Thread BRs). (2) Read channels over the LAN where possible (Hue with key, neoHub). (3) Probe beacon-scans 11-26 and lists meshes. (4) Auto-match mesh to hub by channel + OUI; only ask (dropdown, pre-filled) when two meshes share a channel or nothing matches. (5) Saved answers go into the project's Network Map record so Remotes, Scanner and Site Rig read the same data.

discovery.text: Lutron: mDNS _lutron._tcp. TXT SYSTYPE (HA matches smartbridge*, ra2select*, radiora3*, hwqs*, athena*), DEVCLASS (RA3 081B0101, Caseta SB 08040100, SB Pro 08050100, RA2 Select 080E0401), CODEVER, MACADDR. LEAP TLS on 8081, pairing on 8083. Hostname lutron-<serial>.
Hue: mDNS _hue._tcp (port 443, TXT bridgeid, modelid e.g. BSB002). Keyless GET http://<ip>/api/config gives name, bridgeid, swversion.
IKEA Dirigera: mDNS _ihsp._tcp; local HTTPS API on 8443 (token by pairing button).
Aqara M2/M3: no confirmed Aqara mDNS type. Expect _hap._tcp (HomeKit) and Matter (_matter._tcp); old gateways _miio._udp. Identify by hostname/OUI.
SmartThings hub: Home Assistant matches by DHCP hostname (st*, smartthings*, hub*, smarthub) and MAC OUIs 24:FD:5B, D0:52:A8, 28:6D:97, 68:3A:48.

Somfy TaHoma/Connexoon: _kizbox._tcp (443) always; _kizboxdev._tcp on 8443 only when Developer Mode is on. Name gateway-*, TXT gateway_pin, api_version, fw_version. MAC OUI F8:81:1A. Replaces the port detail in rf.disc.tahoma.
Bond: _bond._tcp, service name starts with the Bond ID; DHCP hostname bond-*; MAC OUIs 3C:6A:2C and F4:4E:38. GET /v2/sys/version needs no token.

Heatmiser neoHub: _hap._tcp named 'heatmiser neohub*'; UDP broadcast 'hubseek' to port 19790, reply hubseek{"ip":...,"device_id":mac}; TCP 4242 (legacy, no token) and 4243 (WebSocket, token). The build's 4242/4243 detection is right; add the hubseek broadcast so it's found even when 4242 is off.

Control4: SDDP NOTIFY ALIVE to 239.255.255.250 UDP 1902 (headers Type, Primary-Proxy, Manufacturer, Model, Driver); Home Assistant also finds Directors by SSDP ST c4:director. Controller/ZAP Type strings are not documented publicly; log what sites send.
Shelly: Gen1 _http._tcp named shelly*; Gen2+ _shelly._tcp; keyless GET /shelly returns model and gen.

Thread border routers: _meshcop._udp TXT nn (network name), xp (ext PAN ID), xa, tv, vn (vendor), mn (model), sb, at, id. Use vn/mn to say 'Apple', 'Google', 'Lutron', 'Aqara' etc. Matter: _matter._tcp (running) and _matterc._udp (waiting to be added).
Sonos: _sonos._tcp (1443, TXT info, vers), SSDP urn:schemas-upnp-org:device:ZonePlayer:1.

subghz_tools.text: rtl_433 decodes Somfy RTS (protocol 167) and io-homecontrol (189). Each event has id = remote address, control = button, counter = rolling code. So it can auto-name 'Somfy remote 1A2B3C pressed Up' with no typing. Tune the SDR so 433.42 MHz is in the passband (e.g. -f 433.42M).

rtl_433 -M level adds RSSI, SNR and noise to every event. -F http serves http://<pi>:8433 with /events (chunked JSON stream) and a WebSocket; -F mqtt also works. The scanner page can read the Site Rig's stream directly.

Portable probe firmware: rtl_433_ESP (ESP32 + CC1101) decodes Somfy RTS as protocol 178 (match by name, not number), tracks noise floor and per-message RSSI, one frequency and one modulation per build, fewer decoders and roughly half the range of an RTL-SDR. OpenMQTTGateway wraps it and reports rssi, currentRssi and rssiThreshold, and can retune live.

Use both. Site Rig Pi + RTL-SDR V4 + rtl_433: the fixed 'ear' that names every remote and logs level/SNR at the rig. ESP32 + CC1101 probe with rtl_433_ESP decode + RSSI: carried to the blind so the reading is taken where the motor's receiver is. The probe's grade (rf.probe.grades) is the pass/fail; the Pi supplies names and the noise picture.
